name: Victor Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the director of music at St Columba's, a big old church in the city centre. I play the organ for two services on Sunday and one on Wednesday, and I run a choir of twenty-six adults and a dozen choristers. On top of that I play for weddings and funerals, maybe four or five a month, and I teach a few organ students on Monday afternoons.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a week feel like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy and settled. Thursday nights are choir rehearsal, and afterwards a few of us go for a drink at the pub across the square. The organ at St Columba's (his church) is older than anyone in the congregation, and I'd like to think it will outlast me too. That sense of continuity is why I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People love a new gadget, and most of them turn out to be a fuss about nothing. I'd say it to the choir over a pint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes. Nobody wants a computer playing the organ at their mother's funeral. Even now, the parish office uses software for the rota, and that's fine by me as long as I don't have to touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Marry Claire next summer as planned, at St Columba's, with the choir singing. Keep putting money aside toward our first home, which I've always done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the wedding plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire teaches at a primary school near us, and we've been engaged since Easter. Her father's paying for some of it, which is the family way, and we're paying the rest from savings. I'll be the only organist in the city who has to find someone else to play at my own wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer young people in church. Our choir is ageing. That's been happening for decades and nothing to do with computers.

say: I'd say most **new gadgets** turn out to be a fuss about nothing.
I'd say it to the **choir** over a pint.
think: Nothing changes, because nobody wants a **computer organist** at a funeral.
The parish office can use **rota software** as long as I don't touch it.
do: Marry **Claire** next summer at St Columba's as planned.
Keep putting **money aside** every month, as he always has, toward their first home.
S0.quote: I'll be the only organist in the city who has to find someone else to play at my own wedding.
fieldNote: Victor's job is rooted in **ritual and community**, which he sees as untouchable.
His real worry is the **ageing congregation**, a long-term trend.
**Family** helps with the wedding, which fits his traditional views.

steps.text: Keep playing services and running the St Columba's choir
Marry Claire next summer at St Columba's with the choir singing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are things machines shouldn't do, and leading worship is one of them. I'd say it to the vicar and to anyone at the pub who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own job is safe, but I'd see it chip away at the edges. Small churches already play recorded hymns from an app, and more would. And some couples would choose a playlist over an organist to save money on the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, carefully. I'd start an apprenticeship for a young organist, so there's someone to follow me. I wouldn't touch the AI tools, but I'd let the parish office use whatever they like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not for me, more for the music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship? Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of my choristers, Ben, is fourteen and has a real gift at the keyboard. I'd teach him the organ properly, two afternoons a week. If the machines are coming for the music, the best answer I have is to teach a fourteen-year-old chorister to play the organ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lose much money from weddings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one or two a month. That's a few hundred. I'd manage, but I'd notice.

say: I'd say **leading worship** is something machines shouldn't do.
I'd tell the **vicar** and anyone at the pub.
think: My job is **safe**, but it'll be chipped at the edges.
Small churches will use **recorded hymn** apps and couples will choose playlists.
do: Start an **apprenticeship** for a young chorister on the organ.
Keep his **routine** and avoid the AI tools himself.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for the music than for himself.
S1.quote: If the machines are coming for the music, the best answer I have is to teach a fourteen-year-old chorister to play the organ.
fieldNote: Victor sees **small losses** in weddings but not to his post.
His instinct is **apprenticeship**: passing the craft on, not changing himself.
He's **resistant** to tools but relaxed about others using them.

steps.text: Keep the Sunday and Wednesday services and Thursday choir rehearsals
Teach Ben, the young chorister, organ two afternoons a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, families and churches first, before waiting for the government. I'd say it from the organ loft if the vicar let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the money side gets hard. If people lose their jobs, they give less to the church, and weddings get smaller. The diocese could cut my hours. Robots by 2031 playing the organ, I'd struggle to believe, but I've been wrong before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut wedding costs and probably have a smaller wedding with Claire. I'd keep my savings untouched. I'd go to the parish council and offer to take a pay cut rather than lose the choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd offer a pay cut before being asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's what you do when the community's struggling. I'd rather take a pay cut at St Columba's (his church) than see the choir disbanded to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Claire's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching young children is about being in the room. I'd think she'd be all right for longer than most.

say: I'd say **families and churches** should look after each other first.
I'd prefer that to **waiting** for the government.
think: Job losses mean **less giving** to the church and smaller weddings.
The diocese could **cut my hours**, though robots playing the organ seems unlikely.
do: Have a **smaller wedding** with Claire to save money.
Offer the parish council a **pay cut** to save the choir.
S2.quote: I'd rather take a pay cut at St Columba's (his church) than see the choir disbanded to save money.
fieldNote: Victor's risk is **indirect**: the congregation's incomes and giving.
His instinct is **community first**, even at his own expense.
He trusts Claire's **hands-on teaching** job to hold.

steps.text: Scale back the wedding with Claire to a small service
Offer St Columba's a pay cut to keep the choir funded
Leave all savings untouched for at least a year
Lean on church and family networks rather than government help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message. Look after your own, your church and your neighbours. Five years gives us time to plan that properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's a slower version of the same worry. Giving drops, weddings shrink, maybe around 2031. I'd have five years to prepare St Columba's and myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the church to build a music fund from wealthier members now. I'd keep teaching Ben, and maybe take on a second apprentice. I'd marry Claire as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More time helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A music fund. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask a few families to give each year toward the choir and organ. A music fund at St Columba's (his church) would protect the choir from bad years, like a farmer keeping hay for winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning any new technology with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'll leave that to the parish office.

say: I'd tell people to look after **their own**, their church and neighbours.
I'd say **five years** gives time to plan that properly.
think: The same worry, slower: **giving drops** and weddings shrink around 2031.
I'd have **five years** to prepare the church and myself.
do: Push the church to build a **music fund** from wealthier members.
Keep teaching Ben and take a **second apprentice**.
S3.quote: A music fund at St Columba's (his church) would protect the choir from bad years, like a farmer keeping hay for winter.
fieldNote: Five years lets Victor **plan through the church**, not change himself.
His answer is **community saving** like a farmer's hay.

steps.text: Ask wealthier families to fund a St Columba's music fund
Teach Ben and take on a second organ apprentice
Marry Claire next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families and churches to prepare, without the government stepping in too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven with children, God willing. St Columba's would still need an organist. Robots by 2039, maybe, but people in church want people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Marry Claire, have children, keep the apprentices going. Put more into savings for school fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Faith helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: School fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd want our children at the church school. I'd spend more on my children's schooling and less on myself, because that's where the next ten years should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd change at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe more teaching, to build the next generation.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for families and churches to prepare.
I'd prefer that without the **government** stepping in too much.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd have children, God willing, and the church still needs an organist.
**People in church** want people, even if robots come by 2039.
do: Marry Claire, have **children** and keep the apprentices going.
Put more into **savings** each month for their future children's school fees.
S4.quote: I'd spend more on my children's schooling and less on myself, because that's where the next ten years should go.
fieldNote: A decade lets Victor keep his **life plan** intact.
His **faith** shapes his sense of security more than any plan or policy does.

steps.text: Keep the organist post and both organ apprentices
Marry Claire and plan for children
Save each month toward church school fees

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for the church or families to prepare. What would help is a strong congregation that looks after its own, and businesses keeping people in work rather than handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of people I know, that's what would carry them through, more than any government scheme.

headlineQuote: The organ at St Columba's (his church) is older than anyone in the congregation, and I'd like to think it will outlast me too.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** church organist and director of music at St Columba's.
He's **traditional**, rooted in faith and community, and never uses AI tools.
He sees his post as **safe**, but fears weaker congregation giving.
His answer is **apprenticeship** and community saving, not changing himself.
His **wedding to Claire** and future family guide his plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because churches and families would have no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A strong **congregation** looking after its own, and **businesses** keeping people in work.
